newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi calls late night talks on Italy metalworkers.
newsitem.headline: Prodi calls late night talks on Italy metalworkers.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi called talks on Sunday with trades union and employers leaders after problems emerged in efforts to settle a pay dispute in Italy's engineering and metalworking industry.

A government source said Prodi would meet leaders of Italy's three main labour confederations, CGIL, CISL and UIL and the employers' umbrella group Confindustria, probably at 2100 GMT after returning from an engagement in northern Italy.
"We hope the talks will serve some purpose," the source said.

Union leaders had hoped for a deal by Sunday in the months-long dispute but said earlier in the day that employers had raised fresh obstacles and called on the government to decide how to carry negotiations forward.
Talks between sectoral unions FIM, FIOM and UILM and the employers' body Federmeccanica resumed last Monday for the first time in more than a month to try to end the dispute.
It involves some 1.7 million workers in a sector which accounts for 40 percent of industrial output.

Newspapers on Sunday reported that the two sides had agreed in principle to graduated monthly wage increases of 200,000 lire ($125), spread over a 30-month national contract period that would replace a two-year contract which expired last June.
But union leaders said Federmeccanica was also insisting that any supplementary factory-level agreements should last for three years to limit the impact on labour costs.
"We have already clarified what our positions our," said CGIL leader Sergio Cofferati. "Federmeccanica has introduced obstacles to the negotiations and it's up to them to remove them."
Any deal is likely to set the tone for other pay accords and prove key to Italy's hopes of containing inflation.

The dispute has focused on differing interpretations of a landmark accord between the government, Confindustria and the labour confederations in 1993 which scrapped automatic inflation-linked wage increases.
Unions say that a three-year contract at factory level would undermine the 1993 agreement.
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu, who has been shepherding the negotiations, appealed to both sides to show a sense of responsibility.
"It would be very risky indeed to prolong this," Treu told Italian radio. "It could lead to a further rise in tension and that is the last thing we need," he said.
